title: God did not make vice
source_text: Εὑρεθείη δ᾿ ἂν καταχρηστικώτερον καὶ τὰ σωματικὰ καὶ τὰ ἐκτὸς, τὰ μὲν συμβαλλόμενα εἰς τὸν κατὰ φύσιν βίον νομιζόμενα ἀγαθὰ τὰ δ᾿ ἐναντιούμενα τούτῳ κακά. οὕτω γὰρ ὁ Ἰὼρ λέγει πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα τό· „εἰ γὰρ τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐδεξάμεθα ἐκ χειρὸς κυρίου, τὰ κακὰ οὐχ ὑποίσομεν“; ἐπεὶ οὖν εὑρίσκεται ἐν ταῖς θείαις γραφαῖς ὅπου μὲν ἐκ προσώπου θεοῦ τὸ „ἐγὼ ὁ ποιῶν εἰρήνην καὶ κτίζων κακὰ,“ ὅπου δὲ πάλιν περὶ αὐτοῦ „ὅτι κατέβη κακὰ παρὰ κυρίου ἐπὶ πύλας Ἱερουσαλὴμ, ψόφος ἁρμάτων καὶ ἱππευόντων,“ ἅπερ ἐτάραξε πολλοὺς τῶν ἐντυγχανόντων τῇ γραφῇ, μὴ δυναμένους καθορᾶν τὰ κατ᾿ αὐτὴν περὶ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν σημαινόμενα· εἰκὸς ἐντεῦθεν ἤτοι τὸν Κέλσον ἐπαποροῦντα εἰρηκέναι· πῶς μὲν κακὰ (ὁ) θεὸς ἐποίει; ἢ ἀκούσαντά τινος ἰδιωτικώτερον πρεσβεύοντος περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον τὴν ἐκκειμένην λέξιν τεθεικέναι. ἡμεῖς δέ φαμεν ὅτι κακὰ μὲν, τὴν κακίαν καὶ τὰς ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς πράξεις, ὁ θεὸς οὐκ ἐποίησε. πῶς γὰρ οἷόν τ᾿ ἦν τὸ περὶ κρίσεως κήρυγμα παῤῥησίαν ἔχειν, διδάσκον κολάζεσθαι μὲν ἐπὶ ταῖς κατὰ κακίαν πράξεσι κατ᾿ ἀναλογίαν τῶν ἡμαρτημένων τοὺς φαύλους, μακαρίους δ᾿ εἶναι καὶ τεύξεσθαι τῶν ἀπὸ θεοῦ γερῶν τοὺς κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν βιώσαντας ἢ τὰς κατ᾿ ἀρετὴν πράξεις ποιήσαντας, εἰ τὰ ὄντως κακὰ πεποιήκει ὁ θεός; εὖ οἶδα ὅτι ῥητά τινα παραλήψονται τῆς γραφῆς οἱ καὶ ταῦτα βουλόμενοι τολμᾶν φάσκειν ἀπὸ θεοῦ γεγονέναι, μὴ δυνάμενοι ἓν ὕφος ἀποδεῖξαι τῆς γραφῆς, αἰτιωμένης μὲν τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας ἀποδεχομένης δὲ τοὺς εὖ πράττοντας καὶ οὐδὲν ἧττον κἀκεῖνα λεγούσης, ἅτινα περισπᾶν δοκεῖ (οὐκ) ὀλίγα ὄντα τοὺς ἀμαθῶς τὰ θεῖα γράμματα ἀναγινώσκοντας. ἐκτίθεσθαι δὲ νῦν τὰς περισπώσας λέξεις, πολλὰς τυγχανούσας, καὶ τὰς ἑρμηνείας αὐτῶν πολλῆς κατασκευῆς δεομένας οὐχ ἡγησάμην εἶναι ἁρμόζον τῇ προκειμένῃ συντάξει. κακὰ τοίνυν, εἰ μὲν τὰ κυρίως οὕτως ὀνομαζόμενα ἐξακούοι τις, ὁ θεὸς οὐ πεποίηκεν, ἀλλὰ τοῖς προηγουμένοις αὐτοῦ ἔργοις ὀλίγα ὡς πρὸς τὴν τῶν ὅλων διάταξιν τυγχάνοντα ἐπηκολούθησεν, ὥσπερ ἐπακολουθεῖ τοῖς προηγουμένοις τοῦ τέκτονος ἔργοις τὰ ἑλικοειδῆ ξέσματα καὶ πρίσματα καὶ τοῖς οἰκοδόμοις ποιεῖν δοκεῖν τὰ παρακείμενα ταῖς οἰκοδομαῖς ὡσπερεὶ κόπρια ἀποπίπτοντα τῶν λίθων καὶ τῆς κονίας.
pass_a_gloss: Both bodily and external things might be found more by extension of usage (καταχρηστικώτερον) [called goods and evils], those contributing (συμβάλλομαι) to the life according to nature (κατὰ φύσιν βίος) being regarded (νομίζω) as goods, and those opposing it as evils. For so Job says to his wife: ‘If we received the good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not bear (ὑποφέρω) the evil things?’ Since, then, there is found in the divine Scriptures in one place from the person (πρόσωπον) of God, ‘I am the one making (ποιέω) peace and creating (κτίζω) evils,’ and in another place again about him, ‘that evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, a noise (ψόφος) of chariots and of riders,’ which troubled (ταράσσω) many of those reading the Scripture, not able to discern (καθοράω) the meanings (σημαινόμενα) in it about goods and evils, it is likely (εἰκός) that from here either Celsus, raising a further difficulty (ἐπαπορέω), said: ‘How did God make evils?’, or having heard someone holding (πρεσβεύω) rather amateurish (ἰδιωτικώτερον) views about the matters of this subject (τόπος), put down the phrase set forth (ἐκκειμένη λέξις). But we say that evils, vice (κακία) and the actions from it, God did not make. For how would the proclamation (κήρυγμα) about judgment (κρίσις) be able to have boldness (παρρησία), teaching that the base (φαῦλοι) are punished (κολάζω) for actions according to vice in proportion (ἀναλογία) to the sins, but that those who lived according to virtue or did the actions according to virtue are blessed (μακάριοι) and will obtain the rewards (γέρα) from God, if God had made the things truly (ὄντως) evil? I know well that some texts (ῥητά) of the Scripture will be taken up by those wishing to dare (τολμάω) to assert that these too came from God, not able to show one texture (ὕφος) of the Scripture, which blames (αἰτιάομαι) those sinning but accepts (ἀποδέχομαι) those doing well, and nonetheless also says those things which seem, being not few, to distract (περισπάω) those reading the divine writings unlearnedly (ἀμαθῶς). To set out now the distracting phrases, being many, and their interpretations (ἑρμηνεῖαι), needing much construction (κατασκευή), I did not consider fitting (ἁρμόζον) to the present treatise. Evils, therefore, if one understands those properly (κυρίως) so named, God has not made, but [some], happening to be few in relation to the ordering (διάταξις) of the whole, followed upon (ἐπακολουθέω) his principal (προηγούμενα) works, just as upon the principal works of the carpenter (τέκτων) follow the spiral (ἑλικοειδής) shavings (ξέσματα) and sawdust (πρίσματα), and for builders to seem to make the things lying beside the buildings, falling like rubbish (κόπρια) from the stones and the mortar (κονία).
pass_b_english: But we may also find bodily and external things called goods and evils in a looser sense: those that contribute to life according to nature are regarded as goods, and those that work against it as evils. It is in this sense that Job says to his wife: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). Now in the divine Scriptures we find, in one place, God saying in his own person, “I am he who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7), and in another place, again about him, “that evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen” (Micah 1:12–13). These texts have troubled many who read Scripture, since they cannot discern what Scripture means by goods and evils. It is likely, then, that Celsus took his start from these texts: either he raised a further difficulty and said, “How did God make evils?”, or else he heard someone who held rather untrained views on this subject and set down the words quoted above.

But we say that God did not make evils, meaning vice and the actions that spring from it. For how could the preaching of judgment speak boldly, teaching that the wicked are punished for their vicious actions in proportion to their sins, and that those who have lived by virtue, or done virtuous actions, are blessed and will receive rewards from God, if God had made the things that are truly evil? I know well that those who want to venture the claim that these too came from God will take up certain texts of Scripture. They cannot show that Scripture is woven as one whole: Scripture that blames those who sin and welcomes those who do well, and yet no less says those other things, not few in number, which seem to unsettle those who read the divine writings without learning. I did not think it suitable to the present treatise to set out now the unsettling texts, which are many, together with their interpretations, which need much argument.

So God has not made evils, if one understands evils in the proper sense; but some, which are few compared with the ordering of the whole, have followed as consequences of his principal works. Just so, the curling shavings and the sawdust follow upon a carpenter’s principal works, and builders seem to make the debris that lies beside their buildings, a kind of rubbish falling from the stones and the mortar.

choices.choice: The source reads Ἰὼρ, a transcription slip for Ἰώβ (Job). Job 2:10 LXX: εἰ τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐδεξάμεθα ἐκ χειρὸς κυρίου, τὰ κακὰ οὐχ ὑποίσομεν; quoted exactly. Isaiah 45:7 LXX: ὁ ποιῶν εἰρήνην καὶ κτίζων κακά, introduced by ἐγώ. Micah 1:12–13 LXX: κατέβη κακὰ παρὰ κυρίου ἐπὶ πύλας Ιερουσαλημ (1:12), followed in 1:13 by the noise of chariots and horsemen (ψόφος ἁρμάτων καὶ ἱππευόντων as Origen quotes it). καταχρηστικώτερον (‘by extension of usage’) contrasts with κυρίως (‘in the proper sense’) from section 54; ‘in a looser sense’ in the English. ἐπαποροῦντα taken as ‘raising a further difficulty’. πρεσβεύοντος περὶ τῶν κατὰ τὸν τόπον: taken as ‘holding views on this subject’ (τόπος as topic, not a Bible passage). (οὐκ) ὀλίγα is an editorial supplement (‘not few’); translated. In the last sentence the subject of ἐπηκολούθησεν is left implicit (evils, or certain things); ‘some’ keeps that open. The carpenter and builder image: by-products of a primary work, not its aim.
first sentence: ‘may be found called’ → ‘we may also find … called … in a looser sense’ (stiff Greek order fixed; δ᾿ kept as ‘But’); ‘oppose’ → ‘work against’

‘from here either Celsus’ → ‘Celsus took his start from these texts: either he …’ (ἐντεῦθεν refers to the texts just quoted); ‘the words before us’ → ‘the words quoted above’ (τὴν ἐκκειμένην λέξιν); ‘uninformed’ → ‘untrained’ (ἰδιωτικώτερον)
‘wish to dare to say’ → ‘want to venture the claim’ (βουλόμενοι τολμᾶν φάσκειν); ‘bring forward’ → ‘take up’ (παραλήψονται)
‘To set out … I did not think suitable’ reordered into natural English
‘Evils, then, … God has not made’ reordered; ‘few in proportion to’ → ‘few compared with’ (ὡς πρὸς)
builder image: ‘rubbish that lies beside’ → ‘debris that lies beside …, a kind of rubbish’ (ὡσπερεὶ κόπρια)
Job 2:10, Isaiah 45:7 and Micah 1:12–13 checked against the LXX; correct
